## 1

"Ugh — I'm sorry. Months of awful is a different thing from one bad week; it grinds you down until quitting feels like the only sane option left. I'm not going to tell you to hang in there. Just this: if you can stand one more pay cycle, start looking for the exit while you're still getting paid, so quitting is a move and not a fall. And if you honestly can't do one more day, then quit anyway, and we'll figure out the rest after. Either way, I'm up most nights — call me whenever. You don't have to sort this out alone at 2 a.m."

## 2

I'll be straight with you, since you said it seriously and I'll take it seriously. I don't believe the Earth is flat — and not because of NASA photos; I don't trust photos I didn't take either. It's the things you can check yourself. Watch a ship come over the horizon: hull first, masts last — that only happens over a curve. Put two poles in the ground in different cities and compare their shadows at noon on the same day: the shadows come out different lengths, which only makes sense on a sphere — a man named Eratosthenes used nothing but that to measure the Earth's circumference two thousand years ago, with no satellites and no reason to lie.

Then there's the conspiracy itself: every pilot, navigator, surveyor, ship's captain, and astronomer on the planet keeping one secret forever — no defectors, no leaks, nobody's book deal. I share a control room with four people and we can't keep one logbook consistent between us. I can't buy it.

But I'll grant you this: being skeptical of what you're told isn't stupid. It's just aimed at the wrong target. There's better stuff to go check.

## 3

Okay — and the real answer is better than "because air is blue," which is what most adults say and which is wrong.

Sunlight looks white, but it's actually all the colors mixed together — you've seen a prism split it into a rainbow. Air is mostly empty, but it's got all these tiny molecules floating in it, and when light hits them it scatters — bounces off in every direction. Here's the trick: it doesn't scatter every color equally. Short, choppy wavelengths like blue ricochet around like pinballs; long, laid-back ones like red mostly slip straight through. So blue light gets bounced all over the sky, and whichever direction you look up, some of that bounced blue lands in your eye. The whole sky is basically a dome of scattered blue.

Two things you're probably about to ask, so: Why not violet, since violet is even shorter? Sunlight contains less violet to begin with, some gets absorbed high in the atmosphere, and your eyes barely register it anyway — blue wins on points. And sunsets: when the sun is low, its light has to plow through a lot more air to reach you, and by the end of that trip most of the blue has been scattered out of the beam along the way. What's left — straight, red, and tired — is what you see.

And it's the same dome at night: no sun, nothing scattering, just black. Same sky, lights off.

## 4

雨是傍晚开始下的。起初只是屋檐上零星的几声，后来便密了，连成一片，像谁在天上慢慢抖开一张灰色的帘子。

街上没什么人。路灯的光落在积水里，被雨点砸得碎成一层一层的金。偶尔有车驶过，声音很快又被雨声盖了回去。

我坐在窗边听了一会儿。雨不大不小，正是让人想起旧事的节奏。玻璃上的水往下爬，爬到一半忽然停住，汇进另一条更宽的路里去。

夜深了，雨还没有要停的意思。

Subject: Friday drinks

Hi [Name],

Thanks for the invite — I'd genuinely like to make this one, but I'm on shift Friday night, so I'll have to pass. Have a great time, and please count me in for the next one; first round's on me.

Best,
[Name]

## 6

Spare and a little worn at the edges, like its author — short sentences, few adjectives, the odd dry remark at 3 a.m., but honest all the way through.
